journal: TRANSPORTATION RESEARCH PART F-TRAFFIC PSYCHOLOGY AND BEHAVIOUR
title: What's your type? A taxonomy of pedestrian route choice behaviour in cities
setting: street (Poznań city-centre street network; walking task from Theatre Bridge to the Old Brewery shopping mall and back, Euclidean distance 1,420 m)
design: mixed (walking task with smartphone GPS tracking + semi-structured in-depth interviews within 48 h; data-driven open coding, topic analysis and Weberian ideal-type typology; authors describe it as a qualitative study)
sample_n: 18 participants aged 20-42 (7 male, 11 female; mean age 23.5) (analytic unit: 36 GPS-tracked routes)
exposure: Perceived noise reported spontaneously in interviews as a 'dynamic element' of the walk: vehicular and tram traffic noise along major streets and noisy crowded areas (mapped in Fig. 4); no acoustic measurement; noise is one of several dynamic elements alongside crowds, weather, sun/shade and time of day
behaviour_measure: Pedestrian route choice on an origin-destination walking task (A to B and back): GPS-recorded routes with distance, duration and speed (Table 1, Figs 3 and 5-9), and interview-reported route decisions and avoidance of noisy/crowded streets used to derive five route-choice types (Table 2)
measurement_method: self-report (in-depth interviews prompted with the participant's GPS track); sensor-GPS-video (smartphone GPS route tracking)
key_finding: Noise emerged as one of the dynamic elements shaping pedestrian route choice: traffic and tram noise was reported to make walking along major streets tiring, the maintainer type (N=4) was characterised as highly sensitive to and avoiding noisy and crowded areas, and the spontaneous type (N=2) as sensitive to noise. The evidence is qualitative and rests on few noise-related quotes; no magnitude or GPS-based comparison of noise exposure is reported.
effect_stats: NR (qualitative; Table 2 dynamic elements: maintainer type N=4 'High sensitivity to weather conditions, time of day, noise, crowded and busy areas'; spontaneous type N=2 'Medium sensitivity to crowded and busy areas; sensitivity to noise'; section 4.1 pedestrian-vehicle interaction topic referenced by 6 participants, e.g. 'I get tired as I walk along major streets because of the traffic and noise' (IDI9, M))

journal: TRANSPORTATION RESEARCH PART F-TRAFFIC PSYCHOLOGY AND BEHAVIOUR
title: Recreational walking decisions in urban away-from-home environments: The relevance of air quality, noise, traffic, and the natural environment
setting: street (hypothetical leisure-time walking route to an unspecified destination in an unfamiliar city; attributes described in text within an online survey)
design: survey (online adaptive choice-based conjoint stated-preference study, Sawtooth Lighthouse 9.6.1)
sample_n: 501 participants (536 completed; 35 removed for stylistic responding; MTurk, quota-matched to 2017 US Census)
exposure: Text-described conjoint attributes with three levels each: noise level (low / medium / high) and noise source (traffic / people / construction), alongside air pollution level and source, natural environment, traffic and time/distance; no acoustic stimuli or sound measurements
behaviour_measure: Stated (intended) leisure-time walking route choice across ACBC tasks (build-your-own, 6-9 screening tasks, unacceptable / must-have questions, 10 three-option choice tasks), summarised as zero-centred hierarchical Bayes part-worth utilities per attribute level and relative attribute importance (%)
key_finding: Participants' intended route choice favoured low over medium over high noise with non-overlapping CIs, and noise level was the third most important attribute (17.04%), statistically on a par with traffic and natural environment but behind air pollution level; people noise was the most tolerated source and construction noise the least. Men placed more weight on noise level and regular leisure walkers more weight on noise source.
effect_stats: Table 3 part-worth utilities (text extraction appears to drop minus signs): noise level Low 45.85 (SD 36.87; 95% CI 42.62, 49.08), Medium 14.30 (SD 21.47; 12.42, 16.18), High 60.15 (SD 43.99; 64.00, 56.30); noise source Traffic 2.72 (SD 17.69; 4.27, 1.17), People 17.04 (SD 16.94; 15.56, 18.52), Construction 14.32 (SD 16.69; 15.78, 12.86). Relative importance: noise level 17.04% (95% CI 16.26, 17.82), noise source 6.23% (95% CI 5.92, 6.55); traffic vs noise level t = 0.63, p = .53; noise level vs natural environment t = 1.41, p = .19 (Section 4.2). Table 4: male gender -> noise level importance B = 3.48, SE 0.82, p < .001, R2 = 0.04; regular walking in leisure time -> noise source importance B = 1.05, SE 0.48, p = .03, R2 = 0.08

title: Effects of environmental sound quality on soundscape preference in a public urban space
setting: park (Sha Tin Park, Hong Kong - 8.05 ha riverside urban park; five locations: North garden, South garden, South garden entrance and two children's playgrounds)
design: survey (on-site objective acoustic and psychoacoustic measurement at five locations + self-administered visitor questionnaire on one weekday)
exposure: Reverse: self-reported visit behaviour (visit frequency, duration of stay, aim of visit) as predictors of soundscape evaluation. Acoustic environment: 10-min Bruel & Kjaer 2270 measurements per location of LZeq, LAeq, LZmax, LAmax, LA10/LA50/LA90, LA10-LA90, and psychoacoustic Neq, Nmax (ISO 532-1) and Seq (Table 2); outcomes: pleasantness, loudness, sound variation and satisfaction ratings, preferences for 11 sound elements and overall preference for a good soundscape (1-5 semantic differential)
behaviour_measure: Self-reported visit frequency (ordinal 1 = monthly to 4 = every day), duration of stay (<30, 30-60, 60-120, >120 min) and aim of visit (reported descriptively only: playing with children 32.0%, sports 24.7%, rest 14.6%)
key_finding: Visit frequency was retained, together with perceived pleasantness and preference for natural sounds, as a positive predictor of overall preference for a good soundscape (beta = 0.18), i.e. more frequent park users expressed stronger preference for a good soundscape, whereas visit frequency and duration of stay were not retained as predictors of soundscape satisfaction. Playgrounds, where human activity raised LAmax and lowered sharpness, were perceived as louder and less satisfying than gardens.
effect_stats: Table 7 stepwise linear regression of overall preference for a good soundscape (n = 150): Visit frequency B = 0.17 (SEB 0.07), 95% CI [0.03, 0.32], b = 0.18, p = 0.017; model R2 = 0.22, F (3146) = 13.9, p < 0.001. Section 3.2: gender, visit frequency, duration of staying and sound variation perception excluded from the satisfaction regression (p >= 0.05; values NR)

title: Experimental study on the effect of background music on pedestrian movement at high density
setting: VR-lab (constructed oval ring single-file corridor in Hefei; central circumference 21.93 m, two 5 m straight sections, width 0.8 m, 3.6 m measurement area; indoor/outdoor not reported)
design: lab-VR-experiment (controlled single-file pedestrian experiment; normal no-rhythm condition vs 120 BPM background music at global densities 0.09-1.82 ped/m; runs of each rhythm condition conducted consecutively, not randomised)
sample_n: 40 college students (18 male, 22 female) (analytic units: runs of 2-40 pedestrians per condition, Table 1; step analysis on 10 selected pedestrians per run, Table 2, and step samples per density, Table 3)
exposure: Background music with no instruction to follow the rhythm: instrumental music of the song 'Faded' (original tempo about 108 BPM) time-stretched to 90, 120 and 150 BPM in Adobe Audition CS6, plus metronome rhythms at 90/120/150 BPM; only the 120 BPM music condition (equal to the normal step frequency of about 2 Hz) was analysed against the normal condition without any rhythm. Playback level and loudspeaker setup NR.
behaviour_measure: Voronoi-based density-velocity and density-flow fundamental diagrams in the 3.6 m measurement area (velocity over 0.4 s intervals); stop-and-go behaviour (stopped if instantaneous velocity < 0.1 m/s), stopping duration distribution, stopping headway and restarting headway; step length and step frequency (per-round step counts from video and step extraction from lateral body sway in trajectories)
measurement_method: sensor-GPS-video (two overhead cameras about 10 m above the floor at 25 fps plus one ground camera; trajectories extracted with PeTrack)
key_finding: With 120 BPM background music, velocity and flow were almost identical to the no-music condition below 1.0 ped/m but lower at medium and high densities, with mean velocity decreases of 2.97%, 1.40%, 20.24% and 37.89% across 0.5 ped/m intervals from 0 to 2.0 ped/m. Pedestrians with music stopped more often and longer (stops beyond 4.6 s +20.76%; longest stop 15.96 s vs 6.52 s at 1.82 ped/m) at higher stopping and restarting headways, and step frequency was lower at 1.37 and 1.82 ped/m while step length did not differ below 1.37 ped/m.
effect_stats: Results, Fundamental diagram [page 3]: mean decrease of velocity with rhythm 2.97%, 1.40%, 20.24%, 37.89% (0-2.0 Ped/m, 0.5 Ped/m intervals); Time-space diagram [page 4]: stopping headway 0.50 +/- 0.11 m (normal) vs 0.51 +/- 0.11 m (music), F-test P-value < 0.05; restarting headway 0.53 +/- 0.11 m vs 0.55 +/- 0.12 m, F-test P-value < 0.05; longest stopping duration 15.96 s (music) vs 6.52 s (normal) at 1.82 Ped/m [page 3]; Table 2: step frequency at 1.37 Ped/m 1.38 +/- 0.15 Hz (normal) vs 1.10 +/- 0.10 Hz (music), F-test P-value < 0.05; Table 4: at 1.37 Ped/m step frequency 1.40 +/- 0.40 vs 1.20 +/- 0.28 Hz (P < 0.05); at 1.82 Ped/m step length 0.22 +/- 0.07 vs 0.24 +/- 0.08 m (P < 0.05) and step frequency 0.95 +/- 0.24 vs 0.88 +/- 0.18 Hz (P < 0.05)

title: Dynamic Perspectives: Spatiotemporal Characteristics and Time-Segmented Environmental Drivers of Public Recreational Behavior in Urban Parks
setting: park (Fuzhou Hot Spring Park, Gulou District — 16.7 hm2 comprehensive urban park; 24 grids with 27 monitoring points classified as path-, areal- and node-type spaces)
design: field-observation (SOPARC-coded 360-degree panoramic camera observation with concurrent audio recording, microclimate and illuminance measurement; 4 summer days, 3–4 and 8–9 September 2022)
sample_n: NR individuals (daily average 2036 visitors recorded; analytic unit: 27 monitoring points observed hourly 06:00–21:00 on 4 days)
exposure: Temporal soundscape recorded concurrently with behaviour observations at each monitoring point (Sony PCM-D100); spectrogram analysis identified dominant sound sources classified as natural sounds (NS; mainly birdsong, 54.3% of recorded sources), traffic sounds (TS; mainly car horns), management sounds (MS; e.g., sweeping) and recreational sounds (RS; e.g., hand clapping, foot stomping). Sound pressure levels and the quantification of source variables not reported. Examined alongside microclimate (temperature, relative humidity), illuminance and stable landscape variables.
behaviour_measure: SOPARC-coded counts per monitoring point per hourly scan (06:00–21:00) of visitors by gender and age group (children, young, middle-aged, older adults) and by activity type: static behaviour — relaxation activities (RA: sitting, reading, meditation), nature engagement (NEA), social interaction (SIA: tea drinking, chatting, playing cards); dynamic behaviour — sports (SA), leisure (LA), facility-based field activities (FA); plus kernel density and Shannon–Wiener diversity of behavioural coexistence and intergenerational co-presence
measurement_method: observation; sensor-GPS-video (360-degree panoramic camera recordings coded with the SOPARC protocol by two trained observers)
key_finding: After FDR adjustment, morning recreational sounds were positively correlated with middle-aged visitor counts and social interaction activities, morning management sounds positively with children's counts, and night-time traffic sounds negatively with middle-aged visitor counts (Figure 12). In time-segmented regressions, morning SIA was explained mainly by recreational sounds (standardized beta = 0.627) and their interaction with green view index, morning leisure activities were negatively associated with management sounds, and recreational sounds strengthened the effect of resting facilities on morning middle-aged visitation; temperature rather than soundscape was the key temporal driver overall.
effect_stats: Table 3, morning SIA (R2 = 0.559, adj R2 = 0.532): RS B = 0.627, SE = 0.098, Beta = 0.627, T = 6.421, Sig. = 0; Z1*RS B = 0.366, SE = 0.096, Beta = 0.377, T = 3.825, Sig. = 0. Table 3, morning LA (R2 = 0.456, adj R2 = 0.421): MS B = −0.487, SE = 0.2, Beta = −0.487, T = −2.437, Sig. = 0.019; S3*MS B = −2.006, SE = 0.384, Beta = −1.023, T = −5.226, Sig. = 0; S2*MS B = 0.539, SE = 0.229, Beta = 0.266, T = 2.353, Sig. = 0.023. Table 4, morning middle-aged adults (R2 = 0.299, adj R2 = 0.255): S3*RS B = 0.319, SE = 0.139, Beta = 0.287, T = 2.293, Sig. = 0.026. Spearman correlations (Figure 12, FDR-adjusted p < 0.05) not given numerically in text; observations per model NR.

journal: GERMAN JOURNAL OF EXERCISE AND SPORT RESEARCH
title: Transforming urban landscapes: characteristics of urban green spaces for year-round green exercise in Germany
setting: park (urban green spaces used for green exercise across Germany; not site-specific, respondents rate UGS in general)
design: survey (online questionnaire via SoSci Survey, snowball sampling through social media and sports federations, Jan-Mar 2024)
sample_n: 408 participants (772 completed questionnaires; remainder excluded for missing data)
exposure: Self-rated importance of natural sounds in urban green spaces for year-round green exercise (single 5-point Likert item within a 12-item natural-elements battery, alpha = 0.88); no acoustic measurement or site-specific sound exposure
behaviour_measure: Self-reported green exercise activity in UGS under different meteorological conditions (precipitation, cold, strong wind, heat, sun radiation; item wording and scale not reported); type of sport practiced (sport clusters such as endurance, strength-based, team and gymnastic sports); GE frequency (typical 2-3 times/week, Table 2)
key_finding: Natural sounds were the most highly rated natural element for year-round green exercise (76.3% rather important). Their importance correlated weakly and positively with green exercise under precipitation (rho = 0.151) and cold (rho = 0.170) but not under strong wind, heat or sun radiation, and natural-element ratings did not differ significantly between sport clusters.
effect_stats: Table 4 Spearman correlation, natural sounds vs activity during meteorological conditions: precipitation 0.151**, cold 0.170**, strong wind 0.076, heat 0.051, sun radiation 0.034 (* p< 0.05; ** p< 0.01); natural elements effect sizes eta2 0.010-0.050 (p.5); sport clusters: 'Only minor but no significant differences' (p.5)

title: Acoustic and economic valuation of soundscape: An application to the ‘Retiro’ Urban Forest Park
setting: park (Retiro Park, Madrid city centre; 114 ha historic urban forest park divided into 7 zones and 2 main paths)
design: survey (on-site visitor questionnaire with contingent valuation payment card, plus sound level measurements at 14 points)
sample_n: 191 participants (240 approached, response rate 79.6%; acoustic unit: 14 sampling points in 9 zones/paths)
exposure: Measured sound levels with a type II SLM (A-weighted, 4 x 30-min per point, second half of August 2015): LAeq 53.4-63.3 dB(A), highest on main paths 1 and 2 (63.3, 62.1) and zone 4 (60.7); perceived hearing and pleasant/annoying rating of 13 sound sources (birds, wind, water, trees, road traffic, loud voices, musicians, sirens, etc.); perceived annoyance and amount of noise pollution during the visit
behaviour_measure: Stated willingness to pay a once-in-a-lifetime donation for a noise reduction programme inside the park (payment card EUR 1-80, interval maximum likelihood model); reason for visit (walk around 51.3%, walk the pet 20.9%, physical activity 18.3%) reported descriptively only
key_finding: Although LAeq exceeded 55 dB(A) in 6 of 9 zones, 75.4% of visitors reported no or low annoyance and most perceived the amount of noise pollution as low or medium. 39.3% were willing to pay for a noise reduction programme (weighted mean WTP EUR 6.36 per visitor), with income the only significant predictor; no association between sound measures or perceptions and WTP was tested.
effect_stats: NR for sound-behaviour relation (WTP modelled only against socio-economic variables: Table 7 constant 1.398, bid -0.132, income 1.418, all significant at 1%; mean WTP 6.36 EUR, 95% CI 4.13-7.08; WTP x income chi2 = 159,328, p = 0.001 as printed)

journal: Journal of Outdoor Recreation and Tourism
title: Perceived importance of and satisfaction with nature observation activities in urban green areas
setting: park (four large urban green areas used for nature observation, 60–150 ha: Paljassaare Bird Conservation Area, Rocca al Mare coastal green area and Kadriorg park in Tallinn; Pornaistenniemi-Lammassaari in Viikki nature reserve, Helsinki; 2–3.4 km nature trails with boardwalks, information boards and birdwatching towers)
design: survey (on-site interviewer-assisted visitor questionnaire, May–July 2018, 20 days, 08:00–21:00; factor analysis and ordered logistic regression)
sample_n: 802 visitors aged 11–85 (Site 1 n=168, Site 2 n=168, Site 3 n=307, Site 4 n=159); listening-satisfaction (A10) model n=528
exposure: Reverse: self-reported visit behaviours (planned duration of the current visit <1 h / 1–2 h / 2–5 h / >5 h; years of visiting history; usual visiting days; yes/no use of nature trail or boardwalk, information boards and birdwatching tower) as predictors of on-site satisfaction with 'listening to nature sounds' (A10, 5-point) at bird-rich coastal and park green areas; no acoustic measurement or sound-source assessment
behaviour_measure: Self-reported planned duration of the current visit (4 categories), length of visiting history (first time to >10 years), usual visiting days (weekdays / weekend-holidays / both), and yes/no use of nature trail or boardwalk, reading of information boards and visiting the birdwatching tower at the site
measurement_method: self-report (on-site questionnaire filled in by respondents with interviewer help or recorded by the interviewer)
key_finding: Visitors planning to stay more than 5 h were more satisfied with listening to nature sounds at the site than those staying less than an hour (ordered logit coef 1.35, OR 3.9, p<0.05), whereas 1–2 h and 2–5 h stays, visiting history, reading information boards and using nature trails/boardwalks (and the birdwatching tower in a 3-site model) showed no significant association. Visitors who usually came on weekdays as well as weekends/holidays rated the general importance of nature observation (listening, watching and learning combined) higher (OR 1.6).
effect_stats: Table 5, A10 'listen to nature sounds' ordinal logistic model (n = 528, p = 0.000), planned duration of visit (base: less than an hour): 1–2 h Coef 0.11, OR 1.1; 2–5 h 0.42, OR 1.5; More than 5 h 1.35**, OR 3.9; Visiting history −0.04, OR 1.0; Reading infoboards 0.06, OR 1.1; Going to nature trails or boardwalks −0.09, OR 0.9 (** significant at 0.05 level); birdtower use effect 'insignificant' in 3-site model (note under Table 5). Table 3 importance of nature observation (n = 637): usual visit times on weekdays, weekend as well as holidays 0.471**, OR 1.6, p = 0.013; on the weekend/holidays 0.244, OR 1.3, p = 0.284; visiting history 0.071, OR 1.1, p = 0.329

journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
title: A Perceptual Structure of Soundscapes in Urban Public Spaces Using Semantic Coding Based on the Grounded Theory
setting: square (four urban public spaces: Guanqian Square and Central Park Square, Suzhou; Peace Garden and Barker's Pool, Sheffield)
design: qualitative (grounded theory; on-site unstructured open-ended in-depth interviews of about 30 min, convenience sampling until data saturation, January-March 2018; open, axial and selective semantic coding in NVivo 12)
sample_n: 23 participants (13 male, 10 female; aged 18-70; Table 1: Suzhou 10 [pilot phase, January 2018], Sheffield 13)
exposure: Everyday in-situ acoustic environments of four urban public spaces, no manipulation; sound sources noted by the researcher (wind, birds, water/fountains, music, cars/traffic, talking, footsteps, children); LAeq measured with a 01dB Solo sound level meter during each interview: Guanqian Square 65.0-68.5 dB, Central Park Square 70.5-75.8 dB, Peace Garden 68.5-70.8 dB, Barker's Pool 59.1-60.7 dB (section 2.1). Reverse pathway: self-described activities and companion/social-relationship types (friends, family, couples) as determinants of soundscape preferences.
behaviour_measure: Interview-reported companion type, reason for visit, current activity and visit habit (Table 2 background questions), coded into activity 'images' by social relationship (friend, family, couple) (section 3.4.2); self-reported coping strategies toward unwanted sounds: tolerance, avoidance by leaving the place, and complaint such as posting online (section 3.3.3)
measurement_method: self-report (on-site in-depth interviews coded by grounded theory)
key_finding: Users' activities, organised by social relationships, shaped soundscape preferences: a 'friend image' was tied to eventful soundscapes (festivals, performances), a 'family image' to relaxing, peaceful nature sounds and a 'couple image' to quietness and a private sound environment, as people preferred sounds that supported their activities (section 3.4.2, section 4). In the forward direction, users coped with unwanted sounds by tolerance (e.g., traffic noise), avoidance by leaving the place, or complaint, although the authors conclude people mostly handled noise at the psychological level (section 3.3.3); no magnitudes are reported.
effect_stats: NR (qualitative grounded-theory coding; activity images in section 3.4.2 and Figure 1 with codes a4, a13, a14, a77, a85, a91, a97, a98; avoidance codes a39, a92; complaint codes a31, a55, a63)

journal: JOURNAL OF THE ACOUSTICAL SOCIETY OF AMERICA
title: Modeling subjective evaluation of soundscape quality in urban open spaces: An artificial neural network approach
country: Germany; Greece; Italy; Switzerland; United Kingdom; China
setting: square (19 urban open spaces in 9 cities incl. squares, gardens, a street, a seashore and a park - e.g. Kassel Bahnhofsplatz, Athens Seashore, Sheffield Peace Gardens and Barkers Pool, Cambridge All Saint's Garden and Silver Street, Beijing Xi Dan Square, Shanghai Xu Jia Hui Park; located in city centres (7), residential areas (5), tourist spots (5) and near railway stations (2), Table I)
design: survey (large-scale on-site questionnaire interviews with concurrent multi-sensor physical measurements; site-level Pearson/Spearman correlations, t-tests and chi-square screening of physical, behavioural, social/demographic and psychological factors, followed by artificial neural network models and an ordinal logistic regression comparison)
sample_n: over 9000 interviewees in Europe and over 800 in China (section II.A); 62-1041 per site (Table I); acoustic comfort evaluation only at 7 sites (2 Sheffield, 5 China)
exposure: Reverse: user behavioural factors recorded at interview (B1 wearing earphones, B2 reading or writing, B3 watching somewhere, B4 movement status sitting/standing/playing with kids/sporting, B5 frequency of coming to the site 1 first time-5 every day, B6 reason for coming, B7 grouping none/1/more than 1 companion; Table II) as predictors of soundscape evaluation. Acoustic context: SPL (dBA, 1-min measurement) plus air temperature, wind speed, humidity and luminance measured with a multi-sensor station immediately before or after each interview; CadnaA-calculated SPL used for prediction maps (section IV)
behaviour_measure: Binary items for wearing earphones, reading/writing and watching somewhere; movement status (sitting, standing, playing with kids, sporting); frequency of coming to the site (5-point, first time to every day); reason for coming (equipment/services, children playing and social meetings, business/meeting/break, social events, passing by); grouping (alone, with 1 person, with more than 1 person) (Table II)
measurement_method: self-report (on-site face-to-face questionnaire interviews; recording mode for observable items B1-B4 not specified in this paper)
key_finding: Behavioural factors had limited, site-specific associations with the subjective sound level evaluation: watching somewhere (7/19 sites), reason for coming (7/16) and frequency of coming (5/19) were significant in at least 5 sites, whereas wearing earphones (0/4), reading/writing (2/19), movement status (2/19) and grouping (4/19) rarely were, and correlation signs varied across sites (e.g. frequency of coming r = -0.11 to 0.15). For acoustic comfort (7 sites) behavioural factors had limited importance, although grouping and movement status were retained as ANN inputs in some models.
effect_stats: Table III (sound level evaluation; Pearson/Spearman r for 3+ scale factors, two-tailed t-test mean differences for 2-scale factors, Pearson chi-square significance level for B6; * p<0.05, ** p<0.01; minus signs recovered from the source PDF because the text extraction dropped them): B5 frequency of coming significant at site 4 -0.10**, site 5 -0.11**, site 6 0.10**, site 7 0.15**, site 9 -0.07* (5/19, 26.3%); B7 grouping site 4 0.12**, site 8 0.10*, site 10 -0.09**, site 14 0.10* (4/19); B4 movement status site 2 -0.10*, site 8 -0.12** (2/19); B3 watching site 3 0.13*, 4 0.30**, 5 -0.31**, 7 -0.18*, 11 0.20*, 12 0.48**, 14 -0.49** (7/19); B2 reading/writing site 6 0.26*, site 14 0.46** (2/19); B6 reason for coming chi-square site 2 0.01*, 4 0.00**, 6 0.01**, 7 0.02*, 8 0.04*, 11 0.00**, 12 0.01** (7/16); B1 earphones 0/4. Acoustic comfort: behavioural factors described only as having limited importance, no statistics (section II.D). ANN inputs including behavioural factors, e.g. Peace Gardens acoustic comfort model with B7: test coefficient 0.79, RMSE 0.103 (Table VIII)

title: Spatial-temporal change analysis of plant soundscapes and their design methods
setting: park (Jinan Forest Park, Jinan - urban park of 69.5 hm2 with 60.1 hm2 green area at the foot of Kuangshan Mountain; 14 plant-space observation points S1-S14 classified as open, semi-open, closed or vertical space, Table 1)
design: survey (on-site LAeq and frequency measurements + researcher soundwalks rating sound-element clarity + interviews with passers-by; descriptive statistics, ANOVA and Spearman correlation)
sample_n: 1260 interviewees (convenience sampling of passers-by at each observation point, 5 females and 5 males in each of 3 age groups, over 3 days; section 2.2) (acoustic unit: 14 observation points measured in April, July, October 2014 and January 2015)
exposure: Reverse: visitor characteristics including self-reported visitation frequency (with age, gender and satisfaction with the park) related to preference ratings (5-point, 1 very dislike-5 very like) for 12 sound elements (bird chirping, frog and insect chirping, leaves rustling, brook babbling, artistic conception of sculpture, talking, children frolicking, singing and dancing, peddling, broadcast, traffic noise, constructing). Acoustic context: LAeq and octave-band levels measured with an AWA 6228-3 analyser in triplicate every 3 h from 6:00 to 18:00 for 3 days per season; soundwalk clarity ratings (-1 to 1) by 3 researchers
behaviour_measure: Self-reported visitation frequency to the park collected in the interview (response categories not reported)
measurement_method: self-report (face-to-face interviews with passers-by, about 6 min each)
key_finding: Visitation frequency was positively correlated with preference for nature sounds (bird chirping, leaves rustling, brook babbling) and negatively with preference for children frolicking; age showed a similar pattern, while gender and park satisfaction were not correlated with sound preference. The authors also attributed the highest LAeq at entrance/square points and the 9:00 LAeq peak at S2 and S11 to human activities such as dancing, but visitor activity was not measured.
effect_stats: Table 3 Spearman correlation of visitation frequency with preference: V1 bird chirping 0.263*, V2 frog and insect chirping 0.110, V3 leaves rustling in the wind 0.300**, V4 brook babbling 0.278*, V5 artistic conception of sculpture 0.017, V6 talking -0.060, V7 children frolicking -0.276*, V8 singing and dancing -0.045, V9 peddling -0.096, V10 broadcast 0.136, V11 traffic noise -0.179, V12 constructing -0.071 (n used for the correlations NR); LAeq differed across observation points and seasons, ANOVA F = 17.092, P < 0.001 (section 3.1, df NR)

journal: Journal of Engineering, Project, and Production Management
title: A Perceived Acoustic Landscape Model for Zhangjiajie National Forest Park
setting: recreation (Zhangjiajie National Forest Park core scenic area, Hunan - Jinbian Creek, Yuanjiajie, Huangshizhai; three acoustic zones: natural sound source area [primeval forest, stream gorge], tourist-intensive area [core viewing area, rest square, viewing platform], traffic impact area [main scenic roads, parking lot and scenic-spot entrance/exit])
design: mixed (four-season day/night microphone-array recordings + on-site Likert questionnaire + camera and positioning-device records of stay time and photo frequency; CNN sound-source classification and attention-based soundscape perception model)
sample_n: NR (numbers of tourist respondents, recordings and tracked visitors not reported; model data split 60% training / 20% validation / 20% test)
exposure: Acoustic environment zone (natural sound source / tourist-intensive / traffic impact area) recorded with an 8-omnidirectional-microphone array (2 m square, 44.1 kHz, >=30 min per sample) in spring, summer, autumn and winter, daytime (06:00-18:00) and night (18:00-06:00); SPL, Leq, A-weighted level, spectral centroid, MFCC/Mel-spectrogram features and CNN-classified source contributions (natural area: flowing water 42%, bird songs 35%; tourist-intensive area: human voices nearly 60% incl. conversations 45% and camera shutter 13%; traffic area: engine noise 58%)
behaviour_measure: Tourist stay (dwell) time and photo-taking frequency at sampling points, derived from tourist behaviour trajectories (operational definitions, units and summary values not reported)
measurement_method: sensor-GPS-video (cameras installed at key locations in the scenic area and positioning devices carried by tourists)
key_finding: Behaviour is addressed only narratively in the Discussion: the authors state that high pleasure/tranquility scores correlated with longer dwell times and higher photo-taking frequency in natural sound areas, and that high interference in traffic zones is linked to a potential reduction in visit duration; no behavioural data or statistics appear in the Results. Perceived soundscape differed by zone, with the natural sound source area highest in pleasure, tranquility and naturalness and the traffic impact area highest in interference (4.39).

title: Study on the correlation between soundscape perception and pro-environmental behaviors in Grand Canal National Cultural Park based on the expert perspective
setting: VR-lab (laboratory audio-visual reproduction of 12 scenic spots in four parks of the Tongzhou Grand Canal Cultural and Tourism Scenic Area, Grand Canal National Cultural Park: Scenic Area of Three Temples and One Pagoda 1.2 ha, Xihaizi Park 14 ha, Canal Park 19 ha riverfront, Grand Canal Forest Park 713 ha; lab 5 x 2.5 x 4.2 m)
design: lab-VR-experiment (audio-visual interaction experiment with expert questionnaire; SEM with mediation analysis)
sample_n: 172 expert participants (180 questionnaires distributed, 172 valid = 95.56%; 88 male, 84 female; 64.5% aged 25-30; 80.2% architecture)
exposure: Photos of four park groupings presented in random order with 16 field-recorded sound sources (Sony PCM-D50, 2-min segments, each normalized to 55 dB(A) via Nor140 calibration and AKG K702 headphones; ambient < 30 dB): natural (birds chirping, insect buzzing, wind, rustling plants), artificial (conversation, entertainment, footsteps, children playing), mechanical (road traffic noise, broadcast noise, mechanical equipment noise) and canal cultural soundscapes (boatmen's songs, traditional folk music, drama, dance, craftsmanship); exposure variable = expert sound source preference ratings (5-point Likert) forming four soundscape perception latent variables
behaviour_measure: Self-reported pro-environmental behaviours on 5-point Likert scales after the listening session: environmentally responsible behaviours ER1-ER4 (comply with environmental laws, advise others against damaging the Grand Canal environment, donate to related environmental activities, handle personal travel waste) and heritage conservation behaviours HP1-HP4 (participate in heritage activities, comply with heritage management measures, take care of buildings and facilities, learn about canal heritage); most items phrased as intentions ('I will ...'); place attachment PA1-PA5 as mediator
measurement_method: self-report (expert questionnaire completed in the laboratory after audio-visual exposure)
key_finding: Perception of natural (beta = 0.235) and canal cultural soundscapes (0.252) positively predicted environmentally responsible behaviours, and natural (0.263), artificial (0.181) and canal cultural soundscapes (0.208) positively predicted heritage conservation behaviours, whereas mechanical soundscapes had no significant direct effect on either. Place attachment mediated the soundscape-behaviour paths (Table 9: full mediation for mechanical soundscape on both outcomes and for artificial soundscape on environmentally responsible behaviours, partial otherwise).

journal: JOURNAL OF THE ACOUSTICAL SOCIETY OF AMERICA
title: Effects of social, demographical and behavioral factors on the sound level evaluation in urban open spaces
country: Germany; Greece; Italy; Switzerland; United Kingdom; China
setting: mixed (19 urban open public spaces in Kassel, Athens, Thessaloniki, Milan, Fribourg, Cambridge, Sheffield, Beijing and Shanghai - squares, gardens/parks, seashore and street sites located in residential zones, city centres, tourist locations and railway stations; Table I)
design: mixed (large-scale on-site questionnaire interviews with interviewer observation of interviewee behaviour and sound pressure level measurement during or immediately after each interview)
sample_n: 10,031 interviewees (Table I site counts 62-1041; text: more than 10,000 interviews; analytic unit: 19 sites analysed separately; earphone analysis only at sites with >10 earphone wearers)
exposure: Reverse pathway: interviewer-observed user behaviours during the survey (wearing earphones, reading/writing, watching somewhere, moving-related activities) together with social/demographic factors (age, gender, occupation, education, residential status) and home sound level evaluation as predictors; outcome = subjective sound level evaluation of the site on a 5-point scale (-2 very quiet to 2 very noisy). SPL was measured per interview but not analysed in this paper; site soundscapes included traffic noise, water sounds, music, church bells, construction/demolition, chatting, children shouting and footsteps
behaviour_measure: Behaviour of each interviewee observed at the time of the interview: earphone wearing (yes/no), reading/writing (yes/no), watching somewhere (yes/no), moving-related activity coded by energy consumption (1 sitting, 2 standing, 3 walking, 4 playing with children, 5 sport) and dichotomised as moving (walking, playing with children, sport) vs non-moving (sitting, standing)
measurement_method: observation; self-report (interviewer observation of interviewee behaviour; questionnaire sound level evaluation)
key_finding: Wearing earphones, reading/writing and moving activities generally had no significant effect on sound level evaluation (reading/writing significant at 2 sites, moving at 2 sites with Spearman rho about -0.1). Watching behaviour differed significantly at 7 of 19 sites, all in Europe: watching people felt quieter at the Athens and Cambridge sites (e.g., mean difference 0.48 at Silver Street) but noisier at Kritis, IV Novembre and Peace Gardens, which the authors attribute to visual-aural interaction.

title: Ecosystem services enhanced through soundscape management link people and wildlife
setting: recreation (Muir Woods National Monument, California; 559-acre old-growth coast redwood forest trail system, ~0.6 km main-trail segment with 19 mitigation signs; >1 million visitors per year)
design: field-experiment (non-randomised paired week-on/week-off signage manipulation over 10 weekly blocks, 14 March-22 May 2016; continuous acoustic recording, calibrated trail counters, walking-speed timing and visitor-intercept survey)
sample_n: 537 survey respondents (55% response; analytic subsets 240 / 434-453 / 453-535); 1,932 timed walking-speed observations (958 sign absent, 974 sign present); acoustic unit: 13 ARUs, 14,040 measured hours (792 site-days in Wilcoxon test; 3,650 hourly observations from 5 counter-ARU pairs in GAM)
exposure: Reverse: educational A-frame signs (e.g. 'Enter Quietly') asking visitors to speak softly, mute phones/electronics and have children walk quietly, placed in alternating weekly blocks (existing quiet signage covered in sign-absent weeks); hourly visitor counts from calibrated trail counters. Acoustic outcome: hourly and daily-averaged background L50 dB(A) from 13 Roland R-05 acoustic recording units 2-250 m from the trails (05:00-21:00). Soundscape perception outcomes: self-reported ability to hear natural sounds, perceived number of bird types, and 6-point soundscape pleasantness (the latter modelled on hourly L50).
behaviour_measure: Visitor walking speed (m/s) timed between visual markers on 9 trail walkways (23.6-59.1 m); hourly visitor count on the trail (log10, calibrated counters) as the crowd/visitation predictor of sound level; the sign-prompted quiet behaviour itself (voice level, electronics use) was not directly measured
measurement_method: observation (stopwatch timing of identified visitors between markers); sensor-GPS-video (calibrated trail counters for visitor counts); self-report (on-site visitor-intercept tablet survey for soundscape perception)
key_finding: Quiet-behaviour signage lowered daily-averaged L50 from 40.8 to 39.6 dB(A) (-1.19 dB(A)), and sound level rose more slowly with visitor numbers when signs were present (500 visitors: 44.0 vs 38.4 dB(A)), an acoustic equivalent of a 20.6% reduction in visitation. Walking speed did not differ between sign-absent and sign-present blocks (1.03 vs 1.01 m/s). Reported ability to hear natural sounds did not differ by treatment, but visitors perceived more bird diversity under mitigation and higher hourly L50 lowered the probability of a 'very pleasant' soundscape rating.
effect_stats: §3.1: daily L50 signs absent 40.8 ± 0.13 vs present 39.6 ± 0.12 dB(A) (mean ± SE), Wilcoxon rank-sum n = 792, W = 85,337, p = 0.016; GAM n = 3,650: log10Visitor Count β = 2.39, F = 880.7, df = 1, p < 0.001; s(Hour, df = 4) β = -0.14, F = 103.8, df = 1, p < 0.001; Treatment β = -0.49, F = 19.1, df = 1, p < 0.001 (Figure 2a). §3.3: walking speed 1.03 ± 0.02 vs 1.01 ± 0.02 m/s, Kruskal-Wallis χ2 = 3.2, df = 1, p = 0.08; ability to hear natural sounds by treatment β = -0.08 ± 0.16, p > 0.05, 95% CI -0.3 to 0.22 (Table 2, n = 199 vs 254); perceived bird types treatment × species β = 0.30 ± 0.14, p = 0.03, 95% CI 0.03-0.60 (n = 240); pleasantness ~ hourly L50 β = -0.18 ± 0.07, p = 0.01, 95% CI -0.32 to -0.04 (n = 453).
